units.title: Reliable Sequential RTL, Reset, and Enables
units.description: Write edge-triggered state updates that behave predictably in simulation and map cleanly to flip-flops.
units.content: Sequential RTL describes state that changes at a clock event, not a sequence of software statements. Use always_ff with a single clock and nonblocking assignments so every right-hand side observes the pre-edge state and all destination registers update together. Blocking assignments remain appropriate for temporary calculations in combinational logic; mixing assignment styles in one state process makes simulation ordering difficult to reason about. Give every register a documented reset policy: asynchronous assertion is useful when immediate clearing is required, while synchronous reset is sampled only on the active clock edge and can simplify timing and implementation. Match reset polarity to the board and cell library, and hold reset active long enough for clocks and power to become stable. Do not assume that deasserting an asynchronous reset close to a clock edge is safe: recovery and removal requirements can be violated, so synchronize release independently in each clock domain. A clock enable should hold the old value when inactive, which is different from assigning zero and different from gating the clock in ordinary RTL. Nonblocking assignment also explains old-value behavior: in a shift register, the second stage receives the previous first-stage value. Use explicit widths and signedness so arithmetic does not silently truncate or extend unexpectedly. A useful review checks reset, enable, and normal-update priority, including simultaneous conditions. Avoid resetting wide datapaths without a real architectural need; reset control state and validity bits when possible, then mark payload invalid until overwritten. Verification should exercise reset assertion and release, back-to-back enables, stalls, and boundary values. Inspect waveforms after each clock edge rather than relying on initial values, because uninitialized state is unknown in four-state simulation. This discipline creates deterministic control without hiding hardware costs.
units.example: module enabled_counter(input logic clk, input logic rst_n, input logic en, output logic [3:0] count); always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin if (!rst_n) count <= 4'd0; else if (en) count <= count + 4'd1; end endmodule
keyPoints: Use nonblocking assignments for edge-triggered state.
Document reset polarity, synchrony, and release assumptions.
An inactive enable holds state; it does not clear state.
Check width, signedness, and simultaneous-control priority.
Reset validity/control state when resetting a full datapath is unnecessary.

test.objective: Check asynchronous reset, enable hold behavior, and modulo-16 counting on rising edges.
test.testbench: module tb_enabled_counter; logic clk=0, rst_n=1, en=0; logic [3:0] count; always #5 clk=~clk; enabled_counter dut(.clk(clk),.rst_n(rst_n),.en(en),.count(count)); initial begin #1 rst_n=0; #1; if(count!==0) $fatal(1,"async reset"); rst_n=1; @(negedge clk) en=1; repeat(3) @(posedge clk); #1; if(count!==3) $fatal(1,"enabled count"); @(negedge clk) en=0; repeat(2) @(posedge clk); #1; if(count!==3) $fatal(1,"enable must hold"); @(negedge clk) en=1; repeat(13) @(posedge clk); #1; if(count!==0) $fatal(1,"modulo wrap"); $display("PASS"); $finish; end endmodule

questions.question: Which assignment best models a flip-flop update in always_ff?
questions.explanation: Nonblocking assignment schedules state updates together after the active event.

questions.question: When does an asynchronous active-low reset assert?
options: Immediately when rst_n becomes 0, independent of clock
Only at a falling clock edge
questions.explanation: The negedge reset event is in the event control, so assertion is asynchronous.

questions.question: What should a register with a disabled clock enable normally do?
questions.explanation: Omitting an assignment on the clock edge infers a hold/enable for the register.

questions.question: In two nonblocking assignments to a shift register, what does stage2 <= stage1 use?
options: The newly scheduled value of stage1
The value after the next clock
questions.explanation: Right-hand sides are evaluated before the nonblocking updates commit.

questions.question: Why can asynchronous reset release be risky?
options: It can violate recovery/removal near a clock edge
It forces the clock to stop
questions.explanation: Deassertion near the edge can leave a flop metastable or violate its timing checks.

questions.question: What is a common safe reset-release strategy in one clock domain?
options: Synchronize deassertion through reset synchronizer flops
Connect reset release directly to every data input
Release reset only when enable is low
questions.explanation: A domain-local synchronizer makes reset deassertion occur safely relative to that clock.

questions.question: What is the effect of assigning zero in the disabled branch?
options: The state clears instead of holding
questions.explanation: An explicit zero assignment is a state update, not an enable hold.

questions.question: Where are blocking assignments commonly appropriate?
questions.explanation: Blocking assignments make combinational procedural calculations occur in source order.

questions.question: Why avoid resetting every bit in a wide datapath without need?
options: Reset networks and resettable cells can cost area, routing, and timing
questions.explanation: Resetting payload bits increases reset fanout and may block efficient memory or flop mapping.

questions.question: Which conditions deserve explicit priority review?
options: Reset, enable, and normal update occurring together
Only the module name and comments
questions.explanation: Nested condition order determines behavior when controls overlap.

questions.question: What does count + 4'd1 produce at count 4'hF when stored in four bits?
questions.explanation: The four-bit destination retains the low four bits, so the count wraps.

questions.question: What does always_ff communicate to tools and readers?
options: Intent to describe sequential logic with single-driver restrictions
Intent to create a combinational latch
That all assignments must be blocking
questions.explanation: always_ff is the SystemVerilog construct for edge-triggered state.

questions.question: What should a reset test first check for an asynchronous reset?
options: State changes while the clock is not required to edge
The design enters a random state
questions.explanation: An assertion between clock edges distinguishes asynchronous from synchronous behavior.

questions.question: Which waveform observation point avoids a same-time-step race after a rising edge?
options: A small delay after the edge or a clocking block sampling region
questions.explanation: Nonblocking updates commit later in the timestep; sampling after them avoids stale reads.

questions.question: What is a clock enable unlike a clock gate?
options: A data/control condition on a clocked register rather than a generated clock
questions.explanation: A clock enable preserves a single clock network and is commonly inferred from conditional state updates.

questions.question: How should signed operands be handled in arithmetic?
options: Declare and size them deliberately to control extension and comparison
Assume every logic vector is signed
questions.explanation: Packed logic vectors are unsigned unless declared or cast as signed.

questions.question: What is a robust response to unknown state before initialization?
options: Reset or establish validity before consuming the value
Treat X as zero in all hardware
Use case equality in synthesized datapath
questions.explanation: Unknown simulation values expose uninitialized state; valid initialization must be designed.

questions.question: Which sequence checks an enable hold most directly?
options: Capture state, disable enable for cycles, then compare state unchanged
Change data only at time zero
questions.explanation: The checker must observe that no update occurred during disabled cycles.

questions.question: What is the best reason to use explicit sized constants such as 4'd1?
options: They clarify width and reduce unintended expression sizing
questions.explanation: Sized constants make the intended arithmetic width visible, though truncation still must be considered.

questions.question: Which state should often be reset when payload memory is left unreset?
options: A valid bit that prevents reading stale payload
Every address bit in the memory array
questions.explanation: Reset validity can guarantee stale data is ignored until a location is written.

units.title: Timing Budgets and Safe Clock-Domain Crossing
units.description: Reason from setup/hold requirements and choose CDC structures that preserve data rather than merely hiding timing paths.
units.content: Synchronous timing is a budget between launch and capture registers. Setup requires data to arrive before the capturing edge with margin for setup time; hold requires data to remain stable after the launch edge for the hold interval. Clock period, clock-to-Q, combinational delay, setup time, skew, and uncertainty all participate. A false path is not a repair for a failing synchronous path, and declaring two clocks asynchronous does not make signals safe to sample. Metastability can occur when an input changes near a destination edge. A two-flop synchronizer reduces the probability that metastability propagates for a single-bit level, but it does not guarantee absolute elimination and does not preserve a narrow pulse. Place synchronizer stages close, avoid logic between them, mark them with implementation attributes where supported, and keep first-stage fanout restricted to the next stage. For pulses, stretch or encode the event with a toggle and detect its change in the destination; for sustained streams, use a properly designed asynchronous FIFO with Gray-coded pointers and synchronizers. Multi-bit buses cannot be synchronized by independently passing every bit through two flops because bits can settle on different cycles and form a corrupt word. Use a handshake that holds data stable until acknowledgement, a bundled-data protocol with timing constraints, or an asynchronous FIFO. Reset release must also be synchronized separately in each clock domain. CDC analysis checks structural intent while static timing checks within-clock paths; both are needed. Define generated clocks, input/output delays, uncertainty, and asynchronous groups accurately. Review reports for unconstrained endpoints because an unreported path is not automatically safe. Estimate slack as required arrival minus actual arrival, then use critical-path reports to locate the delay. A reliable design writes down which clock owns each register and how every crossing transfers either a level, pulse, or coherent word.
units.example: module bit_sync(input logic dst_clk, input logic dst_rst_n, input logic async_in, output logic sync_out); (* ASYNC_REG = "TRUE" *) logic meta; always_ff @(posedge dst_clk or negedge dst_rst_n) begin if (!dst_rst_n) begin meta<=1'b0; sync_out<=1'b0; end else begin meta<=async_in; sync_out<=meta; end end endmodule
keyPoints: Setup and hold are separate timing requirements on synchronous paths.
Two-flop synchronizers are for single-bit levels, not arbitrary buses or narrow pulses.
Use handshakes or asynchronous FIFOs for coherent multi-bit transfers.
Synchronize reset release independently in every receiving clock domain.
Unconstrained paths and inaccurate clock exceptions require investigation.

test.objective: Check that a single-bit asynchronous level reaches the destination after the synchronizer latency and remains stable.
test.testbench: module tb_bit_sync; logic dst_clk=0, dst_rst_n=0, async_in=0; logic sync_out; always #5 dst_clk=~dst_clk; bit_sync dut(.dst_clk(dst_clk),.dst_rst_n(dst_rst_n),.async_in(async_in),.sync_out(sync_out)); initial begin repeat(2) @(posedge dst_clk); #1; if(sync_out!==0) $fatal(1,"reset value"); dst_rst_n=1; @(negedge dst_clk) async_in=1; @(posedge dst_clk); #1; if(sync_out!==0) $fatal(1,"must traverse first stage"); @(posedge dst_clk); #1; if(sync_out!==1) $fatal(1,"second stage latency"); @(negedge dst_clk) async_in=0; repeat(2) @(posedge dst_clk); #1; if(sync_out!==0) $fatal(1,"falling level"); $display("PASS"); $finish; end endmodule

questions.question: What does setup time require?
options: Data is stable before the capturing edge for a required interval
Data changes exactly at the capturing edge
Reset is asserted after every edge
questions.explanation: Setup is the pre-edge stability requirement at the capture register.

questions.question: What does hold time require?
options: Data remains stable after the capturing edge for a required interval
Data arrives one full period early
questions.explanation: Hold protects the capture register immediately after its active edge.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a two-flop bit synchronizer?
options: Reduce metastability propagation probability for a single-bit level
Guarantee no metastability can ever occur
Synchronize a whole data bus coherently
Remove setup constraints from a clock domain
questions.explanation: The first stage may become metastable; the second gives it settling time.

questions.question: Why is a very narrow pulse unsafe through a plain two-flop synchronizer?
options: It may occur entirely between destination edges and be missed
It always turns into a bus
It violates hold in every source register
It changes the destination clock frequency
questions.explanation: A level synchronizer does not guarantee capture of a pulse shorter than the sampling interval.

questions.question: How can a pulse event cross domains reliably?
options: Use a toggle or request/acknowledge handshake with event detection
Pass it through a single combinational gate
Mark it as a false path
Replicate it onto every bit of a bus
questions.explanation: An encoded change persists long enough to be observed and acknowledged.

questions.question: Why not synchronize each bit of a changing multi-bit word independently?
options: Different bits can be captured on different cycles, creating a mixed word
questions.explanation: Independent latency and metastability resolution do not preserve word coherence.

questions.question: Which structure is commonly used for sustained unrelated-clock streams?
options: Asynchronous FIFO with synchronized Gray pointers
A single bit synchronizer per payload bit
questions.explanation: An asynchronous FIFO safely transfers ordered words across independent clocks.

questions.question: What is Gray coding useful for in asynchronous FIFO pointers?
options: Only one bit changes between adjacent pointer values
All bits change on every increment
It removes the need for synchronizers
questions.explanation: Single-bit transitions reduce ambiguity when a pointer crosses domains.

questions.question: What does positive setup slack indicate?
options: The data path meets the modeled setup requirement with margin
questions.explanation: Positive slack means required arrival is later than actual arrival for setup analysis.

questions.question: Why is false-pathing a real synchronous data path dangerous?
options: It suppresses analysis instead of fixing the path
questions.explanation: A false-path exception can hide a real timing failure from reports.

questions.question: What should a clock constraint describe?
options: Clock period, waveform, and relevant uncertainty/source relationships
questions.explanation: Timing tools need accurate clock definitions to compute required arrival times.

questions.question: How should asynchronous reset deassertion be handled?
options: Synchronize release per destination clock domain
Release every domain from one unsynchronized pin
Treat reset as data bus payload
Use a false path and ignore it
questions.explanation: Each domain needs a release synchronized to its own clock.

questions.question: What is the first-stage synchronizer output generally allowed to drive?
options: The next synchronizer stage, with minimal fanout
Many functional outputs and state machines
An asynchronous reset of another domain
questions.explanation: Restricting fanout prevents unsettled first-stage data from affecting logic.

questions.question: What is clock skew?
options: Difference in clock arrival times at relevant registers
questions.explanation: Launch and capture clock arrival times affect setup and hold budgets.

questions.question: What should be done with an unconstrained endpoint report?
options: Find the missing clock or I/O constraint and assess the path
questions.explanation: Unconstrained paths have no meaningful timing guarantee from STA.

questions.question: When is a bundled-data handshake valid?
options: The sender holds data stable while control crosses and the receiver captures it safely
Every bus bit toggles independently without constraint
The data bus is declared a clock
questions.explanation: The protocol preserves data until the synchronized control establishes a safe capture window.

questions.question: What does timing uncertainty model?
options: Margin for jitter and other clock uncertainty effects
The width of the data bus
questions.explanation: Uncertainty reduces the available timing budget to account for clock variation.

questions.question: Which review best complements static timing analysis?
options: CDC structural analysis and crossing protocol review
questions.explanation: STA alone cannot prove that asynchronous transfers preserve event or word semantics.

questions.question: What does recovery/removal relate to?
options: Asynchronous control deassertion timing relative to a clock
questions.explanation: These are reset/set timing checks analogous to setup and hold around an edge.

questions.question: What does a destination synchronizer add to a level crossing?
options: Latency of typically two or more destination cycles
A guarantee of coherent bus sampling
questions.explanation: Each stage adds clock-cycle latency while increasing settling time.

units.title: Pipelining and Fixed-Width Arithmetic
units.description: Partition long combinational paths into latency-aware stages and make numeric width and signedness explicit.
units.content: A pipeline stores intermediate results so a long combinational calculation is divided into shorter clock-to-clock paths. The main benefit is higher throughput: after the pipeline fills, a result may be produced every cycle even though its latency is several cycles. Registers do not automatically make an algorithm faster if valid, control, and data are misaligned. Carry a valid bit alongside each transaction and stall or flush all related stages consistently. When a downstream stage applies backpressure, either use a ready/valid protocol with elastic storage or ensure the entire pipeline can pause without dropping or duplicating data. Pipeline placement should be guided by timing reports: balance logic depth and account for register setup, clock-to-Q, fanout, and routing. Arithmetic width deserves equal attention. For unsigned addition of N-bit operands, the exact sum may need N+1 bits. Signed two's-complement operands need sign extension before widening; concatenation itself is unsigned unless interpreted deliberately. Multiplication result width can approach the sum of operand widths, and a narrow destination truncates high bits. Division, shifts, and comparisons also depend on signedness and sizing rules. Define rounding, saturation, wraparound, and overflow flags as architectural behavior rather than relying on accidental truncation. Parameterized pipelines must handle boundary parameter values, and generate loops must not create illegal zero-width declarations. A simple reference model using wider integer arithmetic can check corner cases. Verification should distinguish input acceptance from output production and compare results after the known latency, including consecutive transactions and stalls. Resetting data registers may be unnecessary when valid bits reset to zero, but every consumer must honor validity. Retiming can move registers during implementation but cannot correct an incorrect cycle-level contract. A good design documents throughput, latency, initiation interval, and stall behavior next to the interface.
units.example: module pipelined_add #(parameter int W=8)(input logic clk, input logic rst_n, input logic valid_in, input logic [W-1:0] a,b, output logic valid_out, output logic [W:0] sum); always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin if(!rst_n) begin valid_out<=1'b0; sum<='0; end else begin valid_out<=valid_in; if(valid_in) sum<={1'b0,a}+{1'b0,b}; end end endmodule
keyPoints: Pipelining raises potential throughput while adding latency.
Align valid and control information with the data at every stage.
Widen operands before addition or multiplication when carry bits matter.
Specify overflow, truncation, rounding, and signedness intentionally.
Check backpressure and reset behavior across the entire pipeline.

test.objective: Verify one-cycle valid/result latency, carry preservation, and that invalid input does not assert output valid.
test.testbench: module tb_pipelined_add; logic clk=0,rst_n=0,valid_in=0; logic [7:0] a,b; logic valid_out; logic [8:0] sum; always #5 clk=~clk; pipelined_add dut(.clk(clk),.rst_n(rst_n),.valid_in(valid_in),.a(a),.b(b),.valid_out(valid_out),.sum(sum)); initial begin repeat(2) @(posedge clk); #1; rst_n=1; @(negedge clk); valid_in=1; a=8'hff; b=8'h01; @(posedge clk); #1; if(!valid_out||sum!==9'h100) $fatal(1,"carry or latency"); @(negedge clk); valid_in=0; @(posedge clk); #1; if(valid_out!==0) $fatal(1,"invalid transaction"); $display("PASS"); $finish; end endmodule

questions.question: What is pipelining primarily used to improve?
options: Clock frequency and throughput by splitting logic
questions.explanation: Shorter combinational paths can support faster clocks; stages can accept new work each cycle.

questions.question: What is pipeline latency?
options: Time or cycles from transaction acceptance to its result
Number of inputs in a module
questions.explanation: Latency measures how long a transaction takes to traverse the stages.

questions.question: What is throughput of a full pipeline often capable of?
options: One result per cycle when initiation interval is one
questions.explanation: A pipeline can overlap transactions after filling.

questions.question: How wide can the exact unsigned sum of two W-bit values require?
questions.explanation: Adding two W-bit unsigned operands can produce a carry-out.

questions.question: How should signed operands be widened before arithmetic?
options: Sign-extend each operand to the intended width
questions.explanation: Sign extension preserves the two's-complement numeric value.

questions.question: What does assigning a wide result to a narrower vector usually do?
options: Truncates bits according to expression and destination sizing
Raises a compile-time overflow exception always
questions.explanation: RTL truncation is not saturation; overflow handling must be coded explicitly.

questions.question: Why pipeline a valid bit with its payload?
options: To identify which cycle's payload represents a real transaction
questions.explanation: The valid marker must remain aligned as data advances.

questions.question: What is an initiation interval of one?
options: A new transaction can be accepted every cycle
The pipeline has one register total
questions.explanation: Initiation interval describes spacing between accepted transactions.

questions.question: What can happen if a stalled pipeline advances valid but not data?
options: Transaction metadata becomes misaligned with its payload
questions.explanation: All state belonging to a transaction must pause or advance together.

questions.question: What does a ready/valid handshake mean when both are asserted?
options: A transfer is accepted on that sampling edge
The producer must discard the data
questions.explanation: Transfer acceptance is conventionally defined by ready and valid high together.

questions.question: How should multiplication result sizing be approached?
options: Account for operand widths and retain needed product bits explicitly
Assume product always fits the left operand
Let the tool choose intended saturation
questions.explanation: Product width can be much larger than either operand.

questions.question: Why use a wider reference model in a testbench?
options: It can expose RTL truncation and overflow mistakes
It forces the DUT to use software arithmetic
It removes the need for assertions
questions.explanation: A wider model can calculate the mathematical result before DUT-width handling.

questions.question: What should accompany a pipeline flush?
options: A consistent policy for invalidating in-flight transactions
questions.explanation: Flush semantics must clear or cancel valid transactions across all stages.

questions.question: Which arithmetic behavior must be specified for fixed-width datapaths?
options: Wrap, saturation, rounding, and overflow behavior where relevant
Nothing, because HDL decides the algorithm
questions.explanation: Language sizing defines bits, not the intended numerical policy.

questions.question: What does sign extension preserve?
options: The signed numeric value at a larger width
questions.explanation: Replicating the sign bit keeps a two's-complement value unchanged.

questions.question: What is a critical path report useful for in pipelining?
options: Identifying the actual register-to-register delay bottleneck
questions.explanation: Timing analysis identifies where logic depth, routing, or fanout limits frequency.

questions.question: What is elastic buffering intended to support?
options: Independent stalls while preserving transaction order
questions.explanation: Elastic stages absorb backpressure without losing or duplicating accepted items.

questions.question: What is a typical safe reset optimization for payload stages?
options: Reset valid bits and ignore payload until valid
Use unknown values as valid data
questions.explanation: Validity can protect consumers from uninitialized payload storage.

questions.question: What can an arithmetic right shift do for a signed value?
options: Replicate the sign bit while shifting right
Always shift in zero regardless of type
questions.explanation: An arithmetic shift preserves sign for two's-complement signed operands.

questions.question: Why test consecutive valid inputs?
options: To reveal throughput, alignment, and off-by-one latency errors
questions.explanation: Back-to-back transactions exercise overlapped operation rather than isolated cases.

units.title: Synchronous Memories and Register Files
units.description: Design memory interfaces with explicit latency, collision behavior, byte enables, and inference-friendly coding.
units.content: A memory is not merely an array declaration; its port count, read latency, write behavior, reset semantics, and collision policy determine whether it maps to embedded RAM or a large bank of registers. FPGA block memories typically favor synchronous reads and writes, so model the intended registered address or registered output explicitly. A combinational read from a large array may require distributed logic and can prevent block RAM inference. A one-write, one-read register file needs clear rules for reading and writing the same address in one cycle: the implementation may return old data, new data, or an unspecified result unless bypass logic defines it. Byte write enables update selected lanes while retaining the others, and address widths should cover exactly the legal depth. Non-power-of-two depths need range checks because unused binary addresses exist. Resetting every word can block memory inference; reset valid bits or control state instead when the application permits. Initialize contents through supported initialization files or a controlled loading sequence, not assumptions about silicon power-up. For dual-clock memories, treat each port's domain and collision behavior carefully; an array does not make CDC safe. Read-during-write semantics can vary among FPGA families and synthesis modes, so consult the actual target documentation and inspect inferred-memory reports. A behavioral model can include assertions for legal addresses and tests for each byte lane, simultaneous operations, and boundary locations. If asynchronous reads are architecturally necessary, a register-file implementation may be appropriate, but estimate mux and flop cost. Keep memory transactions aligned with valid and ready signals. Verification should test data persistence, independent locations, address aliasing, write masking, and documented read latency. Portable RTL expresses behavior first, but inference must be validated on the intended tool and device.
units.example: module sync_ram #(parameter int AW=4, DW=8)(input logic clk, input logic we, input logic [AW-1:0] addr, input logic [DW-1:0] wdata, output logic [DW-1:0] rdata); logic [DW-1:0] mem [0:(1<<AW)-1]; always_ff @(posedge clk) begin if(we) mem[addr] <= wdata; rdata <= mem[addr]; end endmodule
keyPoints: Memory port shape and synchronous latency affect hardware inference.
Define same-address read/write behavior rather than relying on a device accident.
Byte enables preserve unselected lanes; validate address and depth boundaries.
Avoid resetting every memory word when initialization is not required.
Inspect synthesis reports for actual RAM inference and collision mode.

test.objective: Check synchronous read latency, write persistence, and isolation of two addressed words under the stated old-data read-during-write behavior.
test.testbench: module tb_sync_ram; logic clk=0,we=0; logic [3:0] addr; logic [7:0] wdata,rdata; always #5 clk=~clk; sync_ram dut(.clk(clk),.we(we),.addr(addr),.wdata(wdata),.rdata(rdata)); initial begin @(negedge clk); we=1; addr=3; wdata=8'hA5; @(posedge clk); @(negedge clk); we=0; addr=3; @(posedge clk); #1; if(rdata!==8'hA5) $fatal(1,"stored synchronous read"); @(negedge clk); we=1; addr=4; wdata=8'h3C; @(posedge clk); @(negedge clk); we=0; addr=3; @(posedge clk); #1; if(rdata!==8'hA5) $fatal(1,"address isolation"); $display("PASS"); $finish; end endmodule

questions.question: What coding feature commonly supports FPGA block RAM inference?
options: Synchronous read/write behavior matching the memory primitive
Resetting every bit in every word
questions.explanation: Synchronous memory behavior usually aligns with embedded RAM port capabilities.

questions.question: What does read-during-write collision mean?
options: Reading an address while that address is written
questions.explanation: The same location is both accessed for read and write in one operation interval.

questions.question: Why define collision behavior explicitly?
options: FPGA families and coding patterns can return old, new, or undefined data
It has no effect on output data
questions.explanation: Tool/device modes differ; explicit bypass or architecture avoids accidental dependence.

questions.question: What does a byte write-enable do?
options: Updates selected byte lanes and retains unselected lanes
questions.explanation: Write masking preserves data in disabled lanes.

questions.question: What can resetting every memory entry do to inference?
options: Prevent mapping to embedded RAM and require many resettable flops
questions.explanation: Many FPGA RAM blocks do not support arbitrary per-bit reset.

questions.question: What is a likely consequence of asynchronous array reads for a large memory?
options: Mux/distributed logic implementation rather than block RAM
questions.explanation: Many embedded RAMs require synchronous reads, so asynchronous reads may not infer them.

questions.question: How many address bits are needed to index 16 words?
questions.explanation: Four binary bits encode sixteen distinct addresses.

questions.question: What should be checked for a non-power-of-two memory depth?
options: Unused binary addresses and out-of-range accesses
questions.explanation: The address width can represent extra values that are outside the declared depth.

questions.question: What does a synchronous read imply?
options: Read data updates in relation to a clock edge
Read data changes with zero latency at any address transition
questions.explanation: The read result is registered or sampled by the clocked memory port.

questions.question: What should be reviewed in a synthesis memory report?
options: Inferred memory type, width/depth, port mode, and collision behavior
questions.explanation: The report confirms that intended RTL mapped to the expected resource.

questions.question: Why use a controlled initialization sequence?
options: It works when contents cannot be reset or are not initialized in silicon
It guarantees arbitrary RAM contents at power-up
questions.explanation: A loading protocol establishes known contents where hardware initialization is not assumed.

questions.question: What does a dual-clock memory not solve by itself?
options: CDC protocol and safe coordination between its ports
questions.explanation: Storage with two clocks still needs correct ownership, collision, and data-transfer rules.

questions.question: What should a test check for write-mask behavior?
options: Changed lanes update while disabled lanes retain prior values
questions.explanation: A write mask must preserve the content of unselected byte lanes.

questions.question: What is an address aliasing test intended to reveal?
options: Distinct addresses accidentally selecting the same storage location
A reset pulse that is too long
questions.explanation: Writing and reading separate locations can expose dropped or miswired address bits.

questions.question: Why might a register file use flops instead of block RAM?
options: It needs asynchronous reads or many small, flexible ports
It has one synchronous port exactly matching BRAM
questions.explanation: A flop-based mux structure can support port patterns unsupported by embedded memories.

questions.question: What should a consumer do when synchronous read data is not yet valid?
options: Use a valid/latency contract and wait for the read result
Assume old data is always fresh
Treat X as a legal answer
questions.explanation: Registered reads require the interface to communicate or document result timing.

questions.question: What does write-first behavior mean?
options: A same-cycle read returns the newly written data
questions.explanation: Write-first collision mode selects new data for the read result.

questions.question: How can old-data read behavior be changed architecturally?
options: Add an explicit bypass from write data to read output on address match
questions.explanation: Bypass logic explicitly returns the new write data for a same-address collision.

questions.question: Why is parameter boundary testing important for memory RTL?
options: Zero or unusual depths and widths can make ranges or slices illegal
questions.explanation: Generate bounds and packed ranges must remain legal for supported configurations.

questions.question: What is a memory transaction test expected to cover?
options: Persistence, address boundaries, masking, latency, and collision cases
questions.explanation: These cases validate both storage behavior and the interface contract.

units.title: Protocol Controllers and Defensive FSMs
units.description: Build state machines around transaction handshakes, explicit recovery, and observable legal transitions.
units.content: A protocol controller coordinates an ordered sequence of events. Separate state storage, next-state logic, and output decoding when that separation improves readability, or use a carefully complete single-process style while preserving the same behavioral clarity. Enumerated logic states make waveforms and debug reports meaningful; choose binary encoding for compactness or one-hot encoding for timing based on the target and measured result, not folklore. Every combinational path must assign defaults before case branches so missing assignments do not infer latches. Include a default state recovery policy for illegal encodings, and decide whether outputs are Moore-style functions of state or Mealy-style functions of state and inputs. Mealy outputs can respond within a cycle but may glitch if inputs are asynchronous or change during the cycle. Handshake protocols define transfer as valid and ready being high on the same active edge. A producer must keep valid and payload stable while stalled; a consumer must not claim acceptance while unable to store the item. State transitions should use accepted events, not merely raw requests, or a held request may be counted repeatedly. Reset moves the controller to a documented idle state and clears transaction-valid indicators. Timeout and error paths prevent a controller from waiting forever on a missing response. Avoid using a data signal as a clock; synchronous enables are easier to constrain and verify. Assertions can encode stable-while-stalled, no illegal output combinations, and eventual response under stated environmental assumptions. Tests should cover back-to-back transfers, long stalls, simultaneous request and completion, reset in each state, and error recovery. A transition table is a useful design artifact: list current state, event, next state, and outputs. Check that every state/event combination has a deterministic result. Prefer explicit protocol ownership and avoid hidden assumptions about another block's pulse width or reset timing.
units.example: module ready_sink(input logic clk,rst_n,valid_in,output logic ready_out,output logic [7:0] data_out, input logic [7:0] data_in,output logic pulse); typedef enum logic {EMPTY,FULL} state_t; state_t state; assign ready_out=(state==EMPTY); always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin if(!rst_n) begin state<=EMPTY; data_out<='0; pulse<=0; end else begin pulse<=0; if(valid_in&&ready_out) begin data_out<=data_in; pulse<=1; state<=FULL; end else if(state==FULL) state<=EMPTY; end end endmodule
keyPoints: Define a transition table and make every state/event outcome deterministic.
A ready/valid transfer occurs only when both are high at the sampling edge.
Hold payload stable while valid is asserted and ready is low.
Set combinational defaults and provide a deliberate illegal-state policy.
Test stalls, simultaneous events, reset, and timeout/error recovery.

test.objective: Verify a single-cycle ready/valid acceptance pulse, captured payload, and no duplicate acceptance while the sink is full.
test.testbench: module tb_ready_sink; logic clk=0,rst_n=0,valid_in=0; logic ready_out,pulse; logic [7:0] data_in=0,data_out; always #5 clk=~clk; ready_sink dut(.clk(clk),.rst_n(rst_n),.valid_in(valid_in),.ready_out(ready_out),.data_out(data_out),.data_in(data_in),.pulse(pulse)); initial begin repeat(2) @(posedge clk); #1; rst_n=1; @(negedge clk); valid_in=1; data_in=8'h5A; if(!ready_out) $fatal(1,"initial ready"); @(posedge clk); #1; if(!pulse||data_out!==8'h5A) $fatal(1,"accepted item"); if(ready_out) $fatal(1,"full state"); @(negedge clk); valid_in=0; data_in=8'hC3; @(posedge clk); #1; if(pulse||data_out!==8'h5A) $fatal(1,"no duplicate while full"); @(posedge clk); #1; if(!ready_out||pulse) $fatal(1,"return to empty"); $display("PASS"); $finish; end endmodule

questions.question: On which edge is a ready/valid item transferred?
options: An active clock edge where ready and valid are both high
Any edge where valid is high, regardless of ready
questions.explanation: The handshake defines acceptance by simultaneous ready and valid at sampling.

questions.question: What must a producer do while valid is high and ready is low?
options: Keep valid and payload stable until acceptance
questions.explanation: Stability ensures the receiver sees the offered transaction when it becomes ready.

questions.question: What can happen if a state machine transitions on a held request rather than accepted handshake?
options: The request can be counted repeatedly
questions.explanation: A request held across cycles may cause multiple transitions unless acceptance is qualified.

questions.question: Why assign defaults in combinational next-state logic?
options: To avoid inferred latches for unassigned branches
To add reset to every signal
questions.explanation: Every combinational output must have a value on every path.

questions.question: What benefit do enumerated states provide?
options: Readable state intent in source and debug views
questions.explanation: Named states make transition logic and waveforms easier to review.

questions.question: What is a Moore output?
options: An output determined by current state
An output determined only by an input
questions.explanation: Moore outputs depend on state, typically changing after a state transition.

questions.question: What is a potential risk of Mealy outputs?
options: Combinational input changes can cause within-cycle output glitches
They cannot respond in the same cycle
questions.explanation: Mealy outputs depend on inputs as well as state and may change combinationally.

questions.question: What should happen in a defined illegal-state default branch?
options: Recover to a safe state or assert an explicit failure policy
Ignore the condition without output defaults
questions.explanation: A recovery policy makes corrupted state behavior deliberate and testable.

questions.question: When should an FSM count a request as accepted?
options: When the protocol acceptance condition is true
Whenever request is nonzero at time zero
questions.explanation: Controller transitions must follow the protocol's actual transfer event.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a timeout state or counter?
options: Prevent indefinite waiting for a missing response
questions.explanation: Timeout logic provides a bounded error path when a peer never responds.

questions.question: Which encoding choice should guide binary versus one-hot FSMs?
options: Measured area/timing needs on the target device
A universal rule that one-hot is always smaller
questions.explanation: Encoding tradeoffs depend on device, tool, state count, and timing.

questions.question: Why avoid using a protocol data signal as a clock?
options: It creates a difficult generated-clock/CDC and timing structure
questions.explanation: Data-derived clocks complicate timing analysis and can glitch; use synchronous enables.

questions.question: What should reset establish in a protocol FSM?
options: A documented idle state and cleared validity/control state
A payload equal to the next request
questions.explanation: Known control state prevents false transfers immediately after reset.

questions.question: What does a transition table capture?
options: Current state, event, next state, and output behavior
questions.explanation: A transition table makes protocol behavior explicit across state/event combinations.

questions.question: What should a long-stall test verify?
options: Payload and valid remain stable until acceptance
The producer changes data on every cycle
The state machine exits reset immediately
questions.explanation: Backpressure tests check a central ready/valid stability requirement.

questions.question: What is a back-to-back transfer test checking?
options: The controller can accept consecutive items without losing either
questions.explanation: Continuous accepted handshakes expose throughput and state-transition gaps.

questions.question: What does a default branch in a case statement protect against?
options: Unlisted state values and incomplete combinational assignment
questions.explanation: Default handling avoids accidental inferred storage and defines unexpected-state behavior.

questions.question: Why test reset while a transaction is active?
options: To check cancellation and recovery semantics during in-flight work
To prove reset never affects state
questions.explanation: Reset interruption behavior must be understood rather than assumed.

questions.question: What does a consumer's ready signal promise?
options: It can accept the item on the current sampling edge
questions.explanation: Ready indicates storage or downstream capacity for a transfer.

questions.question: Which property is appropriate for a stalled producer?
questions.explanation: This stability property prevents the offered item from changing before acceptance.

units.title: SystemVerilog Interfaces and Packages
units.description: Use shared protocol types and interfaces to reduce wiring errors while keeping synthesis and tool support explicit.
units.content: SystemVerilog packages provide a single declaration point for shared enumerations, parameters, structures, and helper functions. Import packages deliberately, preferably with explicit names or scoped references where ambiguity matters; wildcard imports can create collisions as a project grows. Place packages before modules that use them in compilation order, or use a file list that establishes dependencies. Interfaces bundle related signals and can define modports to describe which signals a producer or consumer drives. A modport is a compile-time view, not an electrical isolation boundary and not an automatic handshake. Clocking blocks are useful in testbenches to define drive and sample skew and prevent races, but their synthesizability depends on the construct and tool. Keep synthesizable interface contents limited to supported declarations and avoid hiding complex behavior in interface tasks unless the flow explicitly supports it. Parameterized interfaces and modports can improve reuse, but ensure widths and directionality are consistent at every instance. A package typedef struct packed creates a compact vector suitable for registers and ports, while field ordering affects packed bit positions and external layouts. Use typedef enum logic with an explicit width for state and protocol encodings. Avoid duplicate copies of protocol constants in separate files; disagreement between producer and consumer is a maintenance defect. Build order and compilation-unit scope differ across tools, so compile the package and interface with the same settings as integration. Interfaces can simplify top-level wiring but may be less portable across older IP, formal, or lint tools; use a wrapper module at boundaries when necessary. Tests should instantiate producer and consumer modports, check packed-field mapping, and compile with the project's actual file list. Treat shared declarations as an interface contract: changes to field order, widths, or enum values may affect software, assertions, waveform decoders, and physical pins. Version and review those changes carefully.
units.example:
package bus_types; typedef struct packed {logic [7:0] data; logic last;} payload_t; endpackage
interface stream_if(input logic clk); logic valid,ready; bus_types::payload_t payload; modport source(output valid,payload,input ready); modport sink(input valid,payload,output ready); endinterface
keyPoints: Packages centralize shared types and must appear before dependent modules.
Modports document interface direction but do not implement protocol behavior.
Packed struct field order determines bit positions and is part of the contract.
Use clocking blocks to manage testbench sampling/drive races where supported.
Check the actual simulator, synthesis, lint, and formal compilation flows.

test.objective: Compile a package and modport connection, then check producer payload encoding and consumer handshake observation.
test.testbench: module tb_stream_if; logic clk=0; always #5 clk=~clk; stream_if link(clk); assign link.valid=1'b1; assign link.payload=9'h14D; assign link.ready=1'b1; initial begin @(posedge clk); #1; if(!(link.valid&&link.ready)) $fatal(1,"handshake"); if(link.payload.data!==8'hA6||link.payload.last!==1'b1) $fatal(1,"packed fields"); $display("PASS"); $finish; end endmodule

questions.question: What is a primary role of a SystemVerilog package?
options: Share types, constants, and functions across design units
questions.explanation: Packages centralize declarations reused by modules and verification code.

questions.question: What must generally be true about compilation order?
options: A package is compiled before units that reference it
Every module must compile before every package
Order never matters to any tool
Interfaces must be compiled at simulation end
questions.explanation: A dependent compilation unit must see the package declaration.

questions.question: What does a modport describe?
options: Signal direction and access view for an interface user
questions.explanation: Modports specify which side drives or reads interface signals.

questions.question: Does a modport enforce ready/valid protocol correctness?
options: No; it describes directions, while behavior must be implemented and verified
No, because it is only a waveform
questions.explanation: A modport does not implement acceptance, stability, or sequencing semantics.

questions.question: What can a wildcard package import risk?
questions.explanation: Importing every name can conflict with declarations from other packages.

questions.question: What does a packed struct provide?
options: A packed vector with named fields
A heap object with dynamic lifetime
questions.explanation: Packed fields are contiguous bits and can be assigned as a vector.

questions.question: Why does packed-struct field order matter?
options: It determines bit positions in the packed representation
questions.explanation: Changing declaration order can alter external bit layout.

questions.question: What is a clocking block mainly useful for in verification?
options: Defining race-free drive and sample timing
questions.explanation: Clocking blocks control testbench timing relative to clock events.

questions.question: What should be checked before using a feature in synthesizable RTL?
options: Support in every required synthesis and downstream tool
questions.explanation: SystemVerilog language support varies across synthesis and integration tools.

questions.question: What is a useful boundary when legacy IP lacks interface support?
options: A wrapper module translating interface signals to ordinary ports
questions.explanation: Wrappers keep modern internal organization while providing portable module ports.

questions.question: Why define an enum with an explicit logic width?
options: Make encoding width and four-state behavior clear
questions.explanation: An explicit base type fixes width and gives enum values logic semantics.

questions.question: What does a package import not do?
options: It does not instantiate hardware or connect signals
questions.explanation: Packages organize declarations; hardware connections occur through instances and ports.

questions.question: Why use scoped references such as pkg::type_t?
options: Avoid broad imports and make declaration ownership explicit
questions.explanation: Scope qualification prevents ambiguity and clarifies where a type is defined.

questions.question: Which area should test interface behavior beyond compilation?
options: Signal direction, field mapping, handshake, and timing
questions.explanation: Compilation cannot prove that fields and protocol signals are connected correctly.

questions.question: What can parameterized interfaces improve?
options: Reuse across widths or protocol configurations
questions.explanation: Parameters allow one interface declaration to represent multiple legal configurations.

questions.question: What should protocol type changes trigger?
options: Review of connected RTL, assertions, software maps, and waveform decoders
questions.explanation: Shared fields and encodings are contracts across many consumers.

questions.question: What is a compile file list responsible for?
options: Providing ordered source dependencies and consistent tool options
questions.explanation: An explicit file list makes package dependencies and compilation reproducible.

questions.question: Can interface signals be assigned from both sides accidentally?
options: Yes; direction and single-driver ownership must be checked
No, modports prevent every misuse in every tool
questions.explanation: Modports help describe ownership but integration and tool checks remain important.

questions.question: Why may a testbench use a clocking block while RTL does not?
options: It is a verification scheduling construct and may not be synthesizable
It is required for all always_ff processes
questions.explanation: Testbench-only timing controls are not generally hardware structures.

questions.question: What should a package function used by RTL avoid?
options: Unsupported constructs or side effects that cannot synthesize consistently
questions.explanation: Shared helper code must obey the synthesizable subset for production RTL.

units.title: Assertions for Temporal Design Intent
units.description: Express cycle-based requirements with immediate and concurrent assertions and understand their sampling semantics.
units.content: Assertions turn design assumptions and requirements into executable checks. Immediate assertions evaluate when procedural execution reaches them and are useful for local conditions, while concurrent assertions describe temporal behavior sampled on a clock. A property begins with a sampling event, often @(posedge clk), and uses implication operators to relate antecedent events to consequent behavior over time. Overlapped implication |-> starts the consequent in the same sampled cycle; non-overlapped implication |=> starts it on the next sampled cycle. Delay ranges and repetition operators express bounded response and stability, but their exact meaning depends on sampled values and vacuity. An implication passes vacuously when its antecedent never occurs, so pair a response property with cover properties or traffic tests that ensure activation. Use disable iff with a well-defined reset to suppress checks while the design is intentionally inactive; asynchronous reset expression behavior should be reviewed with the simulator and property semantics. Assertions should distinguish environmental assumptions from guarantees made by the DUT. In formal verification, assumptions constrain legal inputs and assertions prove outputs or internal invariants; an overconstrained environment can make a proof meaningless. A ready/valid property can require valid and payload to hold while stalled, and a bounded response property can require acknowledgement within a defined number of cycles. Avoid asserting implementation details unless they are architectural requirements, since such checks make refactoring brittle. Bind properties or place them near the interface contract. Ensure widths and four-state comparisons are intentional: case equality in a procedural checker can detect X values, while assertion sampling may treat unknowns specially. Assertions complement scoreboards and coverage; they do not replace stimulus. Report useful messages and keep failures reproducible with a seed and transaction context. Run assertions in simulation and formal flows where possible, and verify that tool options do not silently disable unsupported properties.
units.example: module response_checker(input logic clk,rst_n,req,ack); property p_ack_next; @(posedge clk) disable iff(!rst_n) req |=> ack; endproperty assert property(p_ack_next) else $error("ack missing next cycle"); endmodule
keyPoints: Concurrent assertions sample behavior on an explicitly chosen clock event.
|-> overlaps the consequent cycle; |=> starts it on the next sampled cycle.
Implication can pass vacuously if its antecedent never occurs.
Separate environmental assumptions from DUT guarantees in formal runs.
Use reset disabling and failure messages without overconstraining the proof.

test.objective: Exercise a request with an acknowledgement on the next sampled cycle; the assertion must remain enabled and the test must fail if the response is late or absent. Requires a simulator with concurrent SVA support.
test.testbench: module tb_response_checker; logic clk=0,rst_n=0,req=0,ack=0; always #5 clk=~clk; response_checker dut(.clk(clk),.rst_n(rst_n),.req(req),.ack(ack)); initial begin repeat(2) @(negedge clk); rst_n=1; @(negedge clk); req=1; @(posedge clk); @(negedge clk); req=0; ack=1; @(posedge clk); if (ack !== 1'b1) $fatal(1,"ack was not asserted on the required response cycle"); @(negedge clk); ack=0; @(posedge clk); if (ack !== 1'b0) $fatal(1,"ack did not return low"); $display("PASS"); $finish; end endmodule
test.integrationAssumptions: Requires a simulator with IEEE SystemVerilog concurrent SVA support, including property, |=>, disable iff, and assertion scheduling semantics. Icarus Verilog does not provide the needed SVA implementation; use a simulator such as Questa/ModelSim, VCS, Xcelium, or a comparable SVA-capable tool, and review assertion diagnostics in the simulator log.

questions.question: When does an immediate assertion evaluate?
options: Only after a future clock sequence
questions.explanation: Immediate assertions execute in the current procedural scheduling context.

questions.question: What does a concurrent assertion describe?
options: A sampled temporal relationship across clock events
questions.explanation: Concurrent properties describe behavior over a specified sampling clock.

questions.question: What does overlapped implication |-> mean?
options: The consequent begins in the same sampled cycle
The consequent starts exactly two clocks later
questions.explanation: Overlapped implication aligns the consequent with the antecedent's sampled cycle.

questions.question: What does non-overlapped implication |=> mean for a simple consequent?
options: The consequent begins at the next sampled cycle
questions.explanation: For a simple sequence, |=> advances the consequent by one sampling event.

questions.question: What is vacuous success?
options: An implication passes because its antecedent never matched
A proof of all possible implementations
questions.explanation: No antecedent means the response obligation was never activated.

questions.question: How can an engineer detect a property that never activates?
options: Add a cover property or ensure stimulus reaches its antecedent
questions.explanation: Coverage of antecedent events reveals whether the property was exercised.

questions.question: What is disable iff commonly used for?
options: Suppress a property during reset or an inactive condition
Force the consequent to pass forever
questions.explanation: The disabling expression aborts or disables checking under specified conditions.

questions.question: In formal verification, what is an assumption?
options: A constraint on permitted environment behavior
questions.explanation: Assumptions restrict the input traces considered by the proof.

questions.question: What is an assertion in a DUT proof?
options: A required behavior the tool attempts to prove
A restriction on all possible inputs
questions.explanation: Assertions state properties the design must satisfy.

questions.question: Why can excessive assumptions be harmful?
options: They may exclude the failing behavior and make the proof meaningless
questions.explanation: Overconstraint can remove realistic scenarios from the proof space.

questions.question: Which property describes ready/valid stall stability?
options: If valid and not ready, valid and payload remain stable next cycle
questions.explanation: A producer must preserve an offered item while the receiver stalls.

questions.question: Why choose the assertion sampling clock explicitly?
options: Temporal meaning depends on the event at which signals are sampled
questions.explanation: Sampling event defines the cycles used by temporal operators.

questions.question: What should a bounded acknowledgement property specify?
options: A maximum response interval and behavior when no response occurs
The location of the output pin
questions.explanation: A bounded property makes response latency requirements precise.

questions.question: What does an assertion failure message improve?
options: Debug context and diagnosis of the violated requirement
questions.explanation: A targeted message identifies the failing contract more quickly.

questions.question: What does an assertion not replace?
options: Stimulus, scoreboards, and coverage of relevant scenarios
questions.explanation: Properties check traces, but a verification plan must still exercise and measure them.

questions.question: Why avoid assertions tied to internal encoding unnecessarily?
options: They can make implementation refactoring brittle without protecting the interface contract
They are required for every FSM
questions.explanation: Architectural properties survive implementation changes better than incidental internal checks.

questions.question: What is a cover property used for?
options: Show that a desired sequence is reachable or exercised
questions.explanation: Cover directives ask the tool to find a trace reaching a scenario.

questions.question: What should be reviewed when using four-state signals in assertions?
options: Unknown-value and sampling semantics for the chosen operator
questions.explanation: X/Z behavior can affect whether a property passes, fails, or becomes unknown.

questions.question: How should request/ack properties handle reset?
options: Define reset disabling and the first valid cycle after release
questions.explanation: Reset behavior is part of the property's temporal contract.

questions.question: What makes an assertion useful as executable documentation?
options: It directly captures a reviewable requirement in temporal form
It is hidden from all tools
questions.explanation: A property states a precise requirement that simulation or formal tools can evaluate.

units.title: Constrained-Random Verification and Coverage
units.description: Generate legal varied transactions, make failures reproducible, and measure whether the test plan reached important cases.
units.content: Constrained-random verification explores combinations that directed tests may overlook, but randomness is useful only when stimulus obeys the protocol and results are checked. Define transaction classes with rand fields and constraints for legal ranges, relationships, alignment, and forbidden combinations. Use solve-before ordering only when distribution dependencies are understood; constraints describe legal values and do not guarantee uniform sampling. A seeded run makes a failure reproducible, so log the seed, configuration, transaction index, and relevant inputs. Keep constraints solvable and diagnose randomize() failures rather than silently substituting default values. A driver converts transactions into cycle-accurate pin activity, while a monitor reconstructs accepted transactions from actual handshakes. A scoreboard compares observed results against an independent reference model and must handle latency, reordering if permitted, and reset cancellation. Functional covergroups measure meaningful scenarios such as boundary values, backpressure lengths, operation combinations, and transitions; coverpoints and crosses should be selected from a verification plan rather than maximized blindly. Code coverage indicates executed statements or branches, not correctness or requirement completeness. A high coverage percentage can coexist with untested protocol behavior, while an uncovered bin may be unreachable, missing stimulus, or an invalid requirement. Add targeted directed tests for rare corner cases and use constraints to focus random exploration. Avoid overly restrictive constraints that suppress bugs, and avoid massive crosses whose bins are meaningless. Use assertions for cycle-level invariants and coverage to show occurrence. Regression management should track seeds, tool versions, pass/fail status, and runtime. Minimize failing seeds into small traces before fixing the design. Random stability across tool versions is not guaranteed, so the seed alone may not reproduce across different solvers; preserve the failing transaction sequence when practical. Coverage closure is an engineering judgment tied to requirements, not a score-chasing exercise.
units.example: class txn; rand bit [3:0] addr; rand bit [7:0] data; rand bit write; constraint aligned {addr[0]==0;} constraint useful_data {data inside {[8'h10:8'hEF]};} endclass
keyPoints: Constrain transactions to legal protocol space but retain useful variation.
Record seed, configuration, and failing transaction context for reproducibility.
Check results with an independent scoreboard and monitor accepted handshakes.
Functional coverage measures scenarios; code coverage does not prove correctness.
Investigate uncovered bins and preserve/minimize failing random traces.

test.objective: With a simulator supporting class-based constrained randomization and constraint solving, randomize 100 legal aligned transactions, check constraints every time, and count that a representative address-space range is reached.
test.testbench: module tb_random_txn; initial begin txn t; int seen_low=0,seen_high=0; t=new(); for(int i=0;i<100;i++) begin if(!t.randomize()) $fatal(1,"randomize failed at %0d",i); if(t.addr[0]!==0) $fatal(1,"alignment constraint"); if(t.data<8'h10||t.data>8'hEF) $fatal(1,"data constraint"); if(t.addr<8) seen_low++; else seen_high++; end if(seen_low==0||seen_high==0) $fatal(1,"insufficient address spread; rerun with recorded seed"); $display("PASS seed-controlled randomized constraints"); $finish; end endmodule
test.integrationAssumptions: Requires full SystemVerilog class support, constraint blocks, randomize(), and a functioning constraint solver; procedural loops alone are not a substitute for solver-backed randomization. Icarus Verilog does not provide the required class-constrained-random feature set; use a simulator such as Questa/ModelSim, VCS, Xcelium, or another simulator with constrained-random and coverage support, and record the random seed when diagnosing distribution failures.

questions.question: What is constrained-random stimulus intended to add?
options: Varied legal combinations beyond a small directed set
questions.explanation: Constraints keep generated transactions legal while exploring combinations.

questions.question: What does randomize() returning failure indicate?
options: No satisfying assignment was found for the current constraints
questions.explanation: An unsatisfiable constraint set must be diagnosed, not silently ignored.

questions.question: Why record a random seed?
options: Help reproduce the generated scenario and failure
Guarantee identical behavior across every solver version
questions.explanation: A seed supports repeatability within a compatible simulator and configuration.

questions.question: What else should a failure log preserve beyond seed?
options: Configuration, transaction index, and relevant observed inputs
questions.explanation: Solver or environment changes can make a seed alone insufficient.

questions.question: What does a transaction driver do?
options: Converts abstract transactions into cycle-level interface activity
questions.explanation: The driver applies transactions to DUT pins following the protocol.

questions.question: What does a monitor observe?
options: Actual interface events and accepted transfers
questions.explanation: Monitoring the pins independently verifies what the DUT and environment actually exchanged.

questions.question: What does a scoreboard compare?
options: Observed DUT results against a reference expectation
questions.explanation: A scoreboard checks functional output using a reference model.

questions.question: Why should the reference model be independent?
options: Shared implementation mistakes can make both model and DUT wrong identically
It makes simulation slower by design
questions.explanation: Independent modeling reduces correlated bugs in checker and implementation.

questions.question: What does functional coverage measure?
options: Whether planned scenarios and value combinations occurred
questions.explanation: Functional coverage tracks user-defined behavior bins.

questions.question: What does code coverage fail to prove?
options: That requirements are correct or all meaningful cases were tested
questions.explanation: Execution metrics do not establish functional completeness.

questions.question: What is a coverage cross?
options: A combination of values across multiple coverpoints
questions.explanation: Cross coverage records combinations such as operation type by boundary class.

questions.question: Why avoid indiscriminately large crosses?
options: They create many low-value bins and obscure useful closure
questions.explanation: Meaningless bins increase complexity without improving requirement measurement.

questions.question: What can an uncovered coverage bin mean?
options: Missing stimulus, unreachable behavior, or an incorrect coverage model
questions.explanation: An uncovered bin must be interpreted against intent and reachability.

questions.question: Why constrain address alignment?
options: Restrict generated addresses to protocol-legal boundaries
questions.explanation: Alignment constraints encode transaction legality.

questions.question: Do constraints necessarily make values uniform?
options: No; legal constraints and solver distribution are separate concerns
Yes, every field is uniform by definition
questions.explanation: Constraint legality does not guarantee a desired probability distribution.

questions.question: When is directed testing still valuable?
options: For deterministic rare boundary and corner scenarios
questions.explanation: Directed tests reliably target important corner cases that random search may rarely hit.

questions.question: What is a useful step after finding a failing random seed?
options: Minimize the transaction trace while preserving failure
questions.explanation: A smaller reproducer is easier to understand and retain as regression coverage.

questions.question: How should regression results be tracked?
options: Seeds, configuration, tool version, runtime, and pass/fail
questions.explanation: Reproducible regression metadata enables diagnosis and trend analysis.

questions.question: What should solve-before be used for?
options: Intentional distribution ordering after understanding its effect
questions.explanation: Solve ordering can alter distributions and should express a deliberate modeling need.

questions.question: How do assertions and coverage complement each other?
options: Assertions check correctness; coverage measures whether scenarios occurred
Coverage proves outputs while assertions count lines
questions.explanation: One detects violations and the other measures verification exercise.

units.title: Timing Constraints, Synthesis, FPGA Build, and Debug
units.description: Connect RTL intent to static timing reports, resource mapping, pin planning, and on-board observability.
units.content: Synthesis transforms RTL into a technology-independent or device-specific netlist; implementation then maps cells, places them, routes wires, and checks timing against constraints. Correct RTL is not enough if clocks, I/O delays, generated clocks, uncertainty, and exceptions are missing or inaccurate. Define primary clocks at their actual ports and create generated clocks for divided or derived clocks; do not invent a clock simply to silence a warning. Input and output delays describe external timing budgets relative to interface clocks. Review unconstrained path reports before trusting a timing summary. Setup slack is required arrival minus actual arrival, and negative slack means the analyzed requirement is missed. Hold analysis is separate and may fail on short paths even when setup passes. Synthesis reports reveal inferred memories, DSP blocks, latches, high-fanout nets, and resource use; compare expected structure with actual mapping. Constraints such as false paths and multicycle paths change analysis and must reflect a proven functional protocol, not an attempt to improve a score. FPGA pin assignment must respect device banking, voltage standards, differential pairs, configuration pins, and board wiring. A successful bitstream build does not ensure the pinout matches the board schematic. Use incremental, reproducible builds and record tool/device versions and constraint revisions. On hardware, LEDs and seven-segment displays provide limited visibility; internal logic analyzers capture selected signals around triggers, but probes consume memory and must not perturb timing excessively. Add status counters or sticky error flags for rare events, and expose synchronization/handshake state in a controlled debug interface. Compare simulation, post-synthesis, and on-board behavior using the same reset assumptions and clock rates. When hardware differs, verify the programmed image, clocks, reset release, pin mapping, timing reports, and CDC paths before changing functional RTL. Preserve the failing capture and build artifacts. A useful debug plan predicts expected waveforms, trigger conditions, and what each observation would rule in or out.
units.example: module heartbeat #(parameter logic [23:0] TERMINAL=24'd9999999)(input logic clk,rst_n,output logic led); logic [23:0] div; always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin if(!rst_n) begin div<='0; led<=1'b0; end else if(div==TERMINAL) begin div<='0; led<=~led; end else div<=div+1'b1; end endmodule
keyPoints: Accurate clocks and I/O delays are required for meaningful timing analysis.
Review unconstrained paths, setup slack, hold slack, and critical-path details.
False and multicycle exceptions need architectural justification.
Check inferred resources and pin/bank/electrical compatibility with the board.
Plan hardware observability and preserve exact build/capture evidence.

test.objective: Use a reduced parameterized divider to check terminal count, LED toggle, reset, and restart behavior in simulation before applying device constraints.
test.testbench: module tb_heartbeat; logic clk=0,rst_n=0,led; always #5 clk=~clk; heartbeat #(.TERMINAL(24'd3)) dut(.clk(clk),.rst_n(rst_n),.led(led)); initial begin repeat(2) @(posedge clk); #1; if(led!==0) $fatal(1,"reset LED"); rst_n=1; repeat(4) @(posedge clk); #1; if(led!==1) $fatal(1,"terminal toggle"); repeat(4) @(posedge clk); #1; if(led!==0) $fatal(1,"periodic restart"); $display("PASS"); $finish; end endmodule

questions.question: What does synthesis primarily do?
options: Transforms RTL into a logic netlist and maps recognizable structures
Places physical pins on the board automatically in every case
questions.explanation: Synthesis elaborates and maps RTL into a hardware netlist.

questions.question: What does implementation add after synthesis?
options: Technology mapping, placement, routing, and physical timing analysis
questions.explanation: Implementation realizes the netlist physically on the target device.

questions.question: What must a primary clock constraint specify?
options: The real clock source and period/waveform used by the design
questions.explanation: Static timing needs an accurate clock model.

questions.question: What is an input delay constraint describing?
options: External arrival timing of input data relative to a clock
questions.explanation: Input delay accounts for timing outside the FPGA before data reaches its input.

questions.question: What is an output delay constraint describing?
options: External timing budget after data leaves the FPGA
questions.explanation: Output delay represents downstream requirements and board timing.

questions.question: What does negative setup slack indicate?
options: The analyzed data path misses its setup requirement
questions.explanation: Negative slack means actual arrival exceeds required arrival.

questions.question: Can setup pass while hold fails?
options: Yes; setup and hold are distinct checks
No, they are the same equation
questions.explanation: Short paths can violate hold even if maximum delay meets setup.

questions.question: What should happen before adding a false-path exception?
options: Prove the path is functionally not timed or is safely handled by CDC protocol
Use it to improve the score
Apply it to every failing endpoint
questions.explanation: Exceptions remove analysis and need a sound architectural basis.

questions.question: What is a generated clock constraint for?
options: A clock derived from a primary clock by known logic or division
questions.explanation: Generated clocks preserve timing relationships for derived clocks.

questions.question: What can an inferred-resource report reveal?
options: Whether RAM, DSP, latch, and high-fanout structures match expectations
questions.explanation: Reports expose hardware mapping and resource cost.

questions.question: What is a key FPGA pin-planning check?
options: Pin bank voltage standards and correspondence to board wiring
questions.explanation: Electrical bank requirements and schematic pin mapping must both be correct.

questions.question: Does successful bitstream generation prove the chosen pins match the board?
options: No; constraints can be syntactically valid but electrically or physically wrong
Yes, it proves all board wiring
No, because bitstreams do not contain pins
questions.explanation: Build success cannot validate the board schematic or external connections.

questions.question: What is an internal logic analyzer useful for?
options: Capturing selected on-chip signals around a trigger
questions.explanation: Embedded capture provides visibility into internal signals during operation.

questions.question: What is a tradeoff of adding debug probes?
options: They consume logic/memory and can affect timing or placement
questions.explanation: Instrumentation uses resources and may perturb implementation.

questions.question: What does a sticky error flag provide?
options: Persistent evidence that a transient event occurred
questions.explanation: The flag retains a rare error until software or debug logic clears it.

questions.question: What should a hardware debug plan define before capture?
options: Expected waveform, trigger, and diagnostic interpretation
questions.explanation: Predetermined expectations make captures useful for discriminating causes.

questions.question: What should be compared when simulation and hardware differ?
options: Programmed image, clock/reset assumptions, pin mapping, timing, and CDC
questions.explanation: Hardware integration conditions often explain divergence from ideal simulation.

questions.question: What is a multicycle exception asserting?
options: A path has a valid multi-cycle functional capture relationship
A design has multiple asynchronous clocks
questions.explanation: Multicycle constraints alter required timing and must match actual capture behavior.

questions.question: Why record tool and device versions?
options: Build results and mapping can depend on tool/device database revisions
questions.explanation: Version metadata aids repeatability and diagnosis of implementation changes.

questions.question: What is a useful first response to an unconstrained timing path?
options: Find its clock or I/O relationship and constrain or justify it
Ignore it because no slack is reported
questions.explanation: Unconstrained paths have no verified timing requirement.

units.title: Formal Checks, Lint, and Equivalence
units.description: Combine static analysis, bounded or inductive proofs, and implementation comparison into a disciplined signoff loop.
units.content: Lint, formal verification, simulation, and equivalence answer different questions.
